notes.front: In Copilot Chat, what is a prompt?
notes.back: The input you give Copilot Chat, such as a question; the system adds extra context to it before sending it to the model.
notes.explanation: So the model receives more than your typed words: open files or repository data can travel with them.
notes.example: Like asking a colleague a question while they glance at the files on your screen, but here the extra context is gathered for you automatically.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Application card: GitHub Copilot Chat”, “2. Key terms”
notes.evidence: The input that is provided to GitHub Copilot Chat. The system combines the prompt with additional context (for example, open files or repository data) before sending it to the language model.

notes.front: What is prompt engineering?
notes.back: Writing clear instructions that steer an AI tool such as Copilot towards code that fits your project’s needs.
notes.explanation: The Learn unit sets the goal as code that is correct in syntax, in function and in context.
notes.example: Like writing a clear brief for a contractor, but the contractor is an AI model that reads your words and your files.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “What is prompt engineering?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is zero-shot prompting?
notes.back: A prompt with no examples, so Copilot relies only on what it learnt in training.
notes.explanation: The Learn unit describes Copilot generating code from its foundational training alone in this case.
notes.example: Like asking a cook for an omelette without handing over a recipe, but the cook is Copilot drawing on its training.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “Zero-shot learning”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is one-shot prompting?
notes.back: A prompt that includes a single example for Copilot to follow.
notes.explanation: The Learn unit says one example helps Copilot produce responses that follow your own patterns and conventions.
notes.example: Like showing a new colleague one finished invoice before asking for the next, but the colleague is Copilot.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “One-shot learning”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is few-shot prompting?
notes.back: A prompt that includes several examples for Copilot to follow.
notes.explanation: The Learn unit says well-crafted examples help Copilot understand patterns quickly.
notes.example: Like giving a translator three sample letters in your house style, but the translator is Copilot writing code.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “Few-shot learning”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is role prompting?
notes.back: Telling Copilot to act as a particular kind of expert, such as a security or performance specialist.
notes.explanation: The Learn unit says this can improve the quality and relevance of code for specialised domains.
notes.example: Like asking a reviewer to read your plan “as an accessibility auditor”, but the reviewer is Copilot.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “Role prompting for specialized tasks”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is chain prompting?
notes.back: Building a complex feature through a series of chat turns, each building on the context of the turns before.
notes.explanation: The Learn unit notes that the history grows with every turn, which can become inefficient and costly to process.
notes.example: Like assembling flat-pack furniture one step at a time with a helper, but each step is a new message to Copilot Chat.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “Chain prompting and managing chat history”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides your prompt, what are two kinds of context GitHub says Copilot uses to generate a response?
notes.back: The code in your current file and the chat history (among others).
notes.explanation: The guide lists these as examples of the additional context that accompanies a prompt.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, introduction
notes.evidence: In addition to your prompt, Copilot uses additional context, like the code in your current file and the chat history, to generate a response.

notes.front: With a file of order-handling code open, Maria asks Copilot Chat simply to “add input checks”. The answer names functions from that file. What best explains this?
notes.back: C: the prompt was combined with context such as open files.
notes.choices:
A) Copilot Chat guessed the function names at random
B) Maria’s prompt contained the function names
C) The system combined her prompt with context such as the open file
D) Copilot Chat searched the web for her code
notes.choicesExplained: A: the names came from her file, not chance. B: her prompt named no functions. D: the context described here is the open file, not a web search.
notes.explanation: The system adds context, for example open files, to the prompt before the model sees it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Application card: GitHub Copilot Chat”, “2. Key terms”
notes.evidence: The system combines the prompt with additional context (for example, open files or repository data) before sending it to the language model.

notes.front: In the 4 Ss of prompting, which S means focusing a prompt on one well-defined task or question?
notes.back: Single.
notes.explanation: The Learn unit ties that clarity to more accurate and useful responses from Copilot.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “Principles of prompt engineering”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the 4 Ss of prompting, which S means making instructions explicit and detailed?
notes.back: Specific.
notes.explanation: The Learn unit links detailed instructions to more precise and applicable code suggestions.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “Principles of prompt engineering”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the 4 Ss of prompting, which S means keeping a prompt concise and to the point?
notes.back: Short.
notes.explanation: The Learn unit balances it against being specific: clear, without overloading Copilot.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “Principles of prompt engineering”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the 4 Ss of prompting, which S means using descriptive file names and keeping related files open?
notes.back: Surround.
notes.explanation: Both give Copilot richer context, which the Learn unit links to more tailored suggestions.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “Principles of prompt engineering”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Priya’s single prompt asks Copilot to “build the sign-up form, fix the timezone bug and tidy the README”. Which of the 4 Ss does it break most clearly?
notes.back: D: Single.
notes.choices:
A) Short
B) Surround
C) Specific
D) Single
notes.choicesExplained: A: the prompt is brief; its problem is the number of tasks, not its length. B: Surround is about file names and open files, which the prompt does not touch. C: each request is reasonably explicit; the fault is mixing three of them.
notes.explanation: Three unrelated jobs in one prompt is the opposite of focusing on one well-defined task.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “Principles of prompt engineering”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When writing a prompt for Copilot, what does GitHub suggest giving first, and what next?
notes.back: A broad description of the goal or scenario first, then the specific requirements.
notes.explanation: GitHub’s guide lists this among its tips for prompts that get better responses from Copilot.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Start general, then get specific”
notes.evidence: When writing a prompt for Copilot, first give Copilot a broad description of the goal or scenario. Then list any specific requirements.

notes.front: Tomás wants Copilot to write a function for his booking app. Which prompt follows “start general, then get specific”?
notes.back: C: goal first, then requirements.
notes.choices:
A) “Booking function?”
B) “Returns false if the date is in the past. Takes a room number.”
C) “Write a function that checks whether a room is free on a given date.” then “It takes a room number and a date” and “It returns false if the date is in the past”
D) “Fix it” with the whole file pasted below
notes.choicesExplained: B lists requirements with no statement of the goal. A gives neither a clear goal nor requirements. D is ambiguous about what “it” is and what the result should be.
notes.explanation: It opens with the broad goal and then lists the specific requirements, the order GitHub’s guide recommends.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Start general, then get specific”
notes.evidence: first give Copilot a broad description of the goal or scenario. Then list any specific requirements.

notes.front: According to GitHub’s prompt guide, what three kinds of example can you give Copilot?
notes.back: Example input data, example outputs and example implementations.
notes.explanation: The guide says examples help Copilot understand what you want.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Give examples”
notes.evidence: Use examples to help Copilot understand what you want. You can provide example input data, example outputs, and example implementations.

notes.front: Lena asks Copilot for a function that tidies British phone numbers, but the result mishandles numbers written with spaces or a +44 prefix. What does GitHub’s guide suggest adding to her prompt?
notes.back: B: sample inputs with the outputs she expects.
notes.choices:
A) The words “be careful” at the end of the prompt
B) A few sample inputs in each format, with the output she expects for each
C) A request for a longer answer
D) Nothing: she should accept the suggestion as it is
notes.choicesExplained: A adds no information about the formats. C asks for length, not correctness. D ignores a known fault; the guide suggests iterating when the result is wrong.
notes.explanation: Example input data and example outputs show Copilot the formats she means.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Give examples”
notes.evidence: Use examples to help Copilot understand what you want. You can provide example input data, example outputs, and example implementations.

notes.front: What does GitHub advise when you want Copilot to complete a complex or large task?
notes.back: Break it into multiple simple, small tasks.
notes.explanation: The guide then has Copilot accomplish the smaller tasks one by one.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Break complex tasks into simpler tasks”
notes.evidence: If you want Copilot to complete a complex or large task, break the task into multiple simple, small tasks.

notes.front: Kofi asks Copilot Chat, in one prompt, for a complete invoicing system and gets a muddled answer. What is the best next step?
notes.back: B: ask for one small piece at a time.
notes.choices:
A) Repeat the same prompt until the answer improves
B) Ask first for a function that totals line items, then one that adds tax, then one that formats the invoice
C) Ask for the whole system again in a longer prompt
D) Add “make it perfect” to the prompt
notes.choicesExplained: A and D do not change the size of the task. C keeps the task as large and complex as before.
notes.explanation: Splitting a large task into small tasks and asking for them one by one is GitHub’s advice for complex work.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Break complex tasks into simpler tasks”
notes.evidence: break the process down into smaller tasks, and ask Copilot to accomplish them one by one

notes.front: Why does GitHub advise against asking Copilot “what does this do”?
notes.back: “This” could mean the current file, the last Copilot response or a specific code block.
notes.explanation: The guide’s alternative is to name the target, such as a particular function or your last response.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Avoid ambiguity”
notes.evidence: don’t ask "what does this do" if "this" could be the current file, the last Copilot response, or a specific code block. Instead, be specific

notes.front: How does GitHub suggest avoiding ambiguity when your code uses an uncommon library?
notes.back: Describe what the library does.
notes.explanation: The guide notes that ambiguity can apply to libraries as well as to words such as “this”.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Avoid ambiguity”
notes.evidence: Ambiguity can also apply to libraries: * If you are using an uncommon library, describe what the library does.

notes.front: Sam has three functions open and asks Copilot Chat “why is this slow?”. Which rewrite best follows GitHub’s advice on ambiguity?
notes.back: A: name the function.
notes.choices:
A) “Why is the `loadOrders` function slow?”
B) “Why is this so slow???”
C) “Why is it slow?”
D) “Explain this.”
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D still leave Copilot to guess whether “this” or “it” means a file, a function or its last response.
notes.explanation: Naming the exact function removes the doubt over what “this” refers to.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Avoid ambiguity”
notes.evidence: Avoid ambiguous terms. For example, don’t ask "what does this do" if "this" could be the current file, the last Copilot response, or a specific code block.

notes.front: When getting suggestions as you code, what does GitHub advise doing with your open files?
notes.back: Open any relevant files and close irrelevant ones.
notes.explanation: Copilot uses the open files to understand your request, so they shape the context it works from.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Indicate relevant code”
notes.evidence: open any relevant files and close irrelevant files. Copilot will use the open files to understand your request.

notes.front: In Copilot Chat in your editor, how can you show Copilot which code you mean?
notes.back: Open the file, or highlight the code you want it to reference.
notes.explanation: Both are ways the guide gives of indicating the relevant code.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Indicate relevant code”
notes.evidence: If you are using Copilot Chat in your IDE, open the file or highlight the code that you want Copilot to reference.

notes.front: Which chat participant can you add in Visual Studio Code to supply context manually, and what is the JetBrains equivalent?
notes.back: @workspace in Visual Studio Code; @project in JetBrains editors.
notes.explanation: The guide calls these keywords a way to supply context to Copilot Chat yourself.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Indicate relevant code”
notes.evidence: You can also use keywords to manually supply context to Copilot Chat. For example, you can add the `@workspace` chat participant in VS Code, or `@project` in JetBrains IDEs.

notes.front: According to the Learn unit, what else in your editor does Copilot draw on for context about the code you are writing?
notes.back: Other files open in parallel tabs.
notes.explanation: The unit mentions it under the Surround principle of keeping related files open.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “Provide enough context with details”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Ana has a dozen unrelated files open while Copilot suggests code for her payment module, and suggestions keep borrowing names from a logging script. What should she try first?
notes.back: A: close unrelated files and open the relevant ones.
notes.choices:
A) Close the unrelated files and open the ones for the payment module
B) Rename the logging script
C) Turn off inline suggestions for the language
D) Open even more files so Copilot has more to choose from
notes.choicesExplained: B hides the symptom without changing what Copilot reads. C removes the help altogether. D adds more irrelevant context, the opposite of the advice.
notes.explanation: Copilot uses open files to understand the request, so unrelated open files feed it unrelated context.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Indicate relevant code”
notes.evidence: open any relevant files and close irrelevant files. Copilot will use the open files to understand your request.

notes.front: If an inline suggestion is not what you wanted, what two options does GitHub’s guide give?
notes.back: Delete it entirely and start over, or keep it and request modifications.
notes.explanation: Both are forms of the guide’s advice to iterate on the prompt and try again.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Experiment and iterate”
notes.evidence: If you are using Copilot to get suggestions as you code, you can delete the suggestion entirely and start over. Or you can keep the suggestion and request modifications.

notes.front: In Copilot Chat, what two options does the guide give when a response misses the mark?
notes.back: Reference the previous response in your next request, or delete it and start over.
notes.explanation: Both follow from the advice to iterate on your prompt rather than accept a poor result.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Experiment and iterate”
notes.evidence: If you are using Copilot Chat, you can reference the previous response in your next request. Or, you can delete the previous response and start over.

notes.front: Chen’s Copilot Chat answer is right except that it uses recursion, which he wants to avoid. Which follow-up best matches GitHub’s advice on iterating?
notes.back: B: refer to the last response and ask for the change.
notes.choices:
A) Accept the answer and rewrite it by hand without telling Copilot
B) “In your last response, replace the recursion with a loop and keep everything else the same.”
C) “Try again.”
D) Start a new thread and ask an unrelated question
notes.choicesExplained: A abandons iteration altogether. C gives Copilot nothing about what to change. D throws away the context he needs.
notes.explanation: Referencing the previous response in the next request keeps the good parts and changes only what is wrong.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Experiment and iterate”
notes.evidence: If you are using Copilot Chat, you can reference the previous response in your next request.

notes.front: Why does it matter what is in your Copilot Chat history?
notes.back: Copilot Chat uses the chat history to get context about your request.
notes.explanation: Old, irrelevant turns therefore become part of the context for new questions.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Keep history relevant”
notes.evidence: Copilot Chat uses the chat history to get context about your request. To give Copilot only the relevant history

notes.front: What does GitHub suggest when you begin a new task in Copilot Chat?
notes.back: Use a thread to start a new conversation for it.
notes.explanation: A new thread gives Copilot only the history relevant to the new task.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Keep history relevant”
notes.evidence: To give Copilot only the relevant history: * Use threads to start a new conversation for a new task

notes.front: To keep chat history relevant, delete requests that are {{c1::no longer relevant or that did not give you the desired result}}.
notes.back: No longer relevant, or did not give you the desired result.
notes.explanation: Removing them keeps them out of the history Copilot Chat uses as context.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Keep history relevant”
notes.evidence: Delete requests that are no longer relevant or that didn’t give you the desired result

notes.front: After an hour debugging a date parser in Copilot Chat, Ifeoma wants help writing a Dockerfile. What does GitHub’s guide suggest?
notes.back: C: start a new thread for the new task.
notes.choices:
A) Carry on in the same conversation so Copilot remembers everything
B) Paste the parser code again before asking
C) Start a new conversation in a thread
D) Ask about the Dockerfile inside a comment in the parser file
notes.choicesExplained: A and B keep irrelevant history in play. D mixes the new task into unrelated code, the kind of ambiguity the guide warns against.
notes.explanation: A new conversation keeps the long parser discussion out of the context for the Dockerfile.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Keep history relevant”
notes.evidence: Use threads to start a new conversation for a new task

notes.front: What are two ways the Learn unit suggests keeping a long chain of chat turns efficient?
notes.back: Any two: summarise the context so far; reset with only the essential details; refer briefly to earlier work instead of repeating it.
notes.explanation: Long histories become costly to process, which the unit sets against the value of detailed context.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “Chain prompting and managing chat history”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When Copilot’s suggestions or explanations for your codebase disappoint, what are two coding practices GitHub suggests checking?
notes.back: Any two, among others: a consistent code style, descriptive names, comments in the code, modular scoped components.
notes.explanation: The guide asks you to make sure your existing code follows best practices and is easy to read.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Prompt engineering for GitHub Copilot Chat”, “Follow good coding practices”
notes.evidence: make sure that your existing code follows best practices and is easy to read. For example: * Use a consistent code style and patterns * Use descriptive names for variables and functions * Comment your code

notes.front: In Copilot Chat in Visual Studio Code, how can you see which files Copilot used to generate a response?
notes.back: Open the Used n references dropdown at the top of the response.
notes.explanation: The list may also include your repository’s custom instructions file.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Asking GitHub Copilot questions in your IDE”, “Submitting prompts”
notes.evidence: To see the files that Copilot Chat used to generate the response, select the **Used *n* references** dropdown at the top of the response. The references may include a link to a custom instructions file for your repository.

notes.front: For what kind of work does the Learn unit call zero-shot prompting ideal?
notes.back: Quickly implementing common patterns and standard functionality.
notes.explanation: Zero-shot relies only on Copilot’s foundational training, with no examples in the prompt.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “Zero-shot learning”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What kind of code does the Learn unit say few-shot prompting is especially good at producing?
notes.back: Sophisticated implementations that cope with many different scenarios, including awkward boundary cases.
notes.explanation: The unit places few-shot between the unpredictability of zero-shot and the precision of fine-tuning.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “Few-shot learning”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Grace needs a routine function that turns an article title into a web-address slug. She writes only a comment describing it, with no sample code. Which technique is she using?
notes.back: A: zero-shot prompting.
notes.choices:
A) Zero-shot prompting
B) One-shot prompting
C) Few-shot prompting
D) Role prompting
notes.choicesExplained: B and C need one or several examples in the prompt; she gave none. D would ask Copilot to act as a kind of expert, which she did not do.
notes.explanation: No example is given, so Copilot works from its training alone, which suits a common pattern like this.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “Zero-shot learning”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Dmitri pastes three existing validator functions from his codebase and asks Copilot for a fourth in the same style. Which technique is this?
notes.back: B: few-shot prompting.
notes.choices:
A) Zero-shot prompting
B) Few-shot prompting
C) One-shot prompting
D) Chain prompting
notes.choicesExplained: A uses no example. C uses exactly one. D is a sequence of chat turns building on each other, not a set of examples.
notes.explanation: Several examples in the prompt is what defines few-shot prompting.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “Few-shot learning”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Yusuf is building a web form that must work well with screen readers. Which opening line is an example of role prompting?
notes.back: A: “Act as an accessibility specialist…”
notes.choices:
A) “Act as an accessibility specialist and build a sign-up form that works with screen readers.”
B) “Write a form.”
C) “Summarise our chat so far, then continue.”
D) “Here are two forms I built earlier; write a third like them.”
notes.choicesExplained: D is few-shot prompting with examples. B is a bare zero-shot request. C manages chat history rather than assigning a role.
notes.explanation: Role prompting asks Copilot to take the perspective of a particular kind of expert.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “Role prompting for specialized tasks”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What separates zero-shot prompting from few-shot prompting?
notes.back: Zero-shot gives Copilot no examples; few-shot gives it several to follow.
notes.explanation: With no examples, zero-shot leans on Copilot’s training alone, while few-shot shows it the patterns you want.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Prompt engineering foundations and best practices” (2025), “How Copilot learns from your prompts”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
